chapters.title: Chapter 1
chapters.html:
The towering white marble gates of Kremnos caught the last of the afternoon sun, their polished surface gleaming like bone. Phainon had been standing in front of them for what felt like hours now, though it was probably closer to twenty minutes. Twenty minutes of polite smiles, casual pleasantries, and answering the same questions phrased six different ways.

His back ached. His neck was starting to prickle under the heat of the sun. The guards still hadn’t budged.

The one leading the questioning was a thick-necked man with a scowl that looked carved from stone, his leather breastplate catching dull flashes of light as he shifted. He hadn’t asked for Phainon’s name again—he already knew that. What he wanted was a reason.

“So then,” the guard drawled, his gaze flicking over Phainon’s borrowed Kremnoan clothes with thinly veiled suspicion, “state your purpose in Castrum Kremnos.”

Phainon smiled, as if this weren’t the sixth time he’d been asked a version of that same thing.

“Just passing through,” he said lightly. “Thought I’d see the sights. No official business.”

The guard stared at him. A long, heavy kind of stare, the kind meant to make a man sweat. Phainon held the look, kept his expression relaxed, though he could feel the itch of tension in his jaw.

He wasn’t sure if it was the clothes Cipher had gotten for him, or if he just didn’t wear the Kremnoan look well enough. Maybe it was the fact that, even dressed like this, something about him would always scream outsider.

The guard opened his mouth, clearly gearing up to press further, maybe deny him outright, when another soldier laid a hand on his shoulder. A brief, silent exchange passed between them. The guard’s jaw ticked. He made a low sound in the back of his throat, then reluctantly stepped aside.

Phainon smiled, dipping his head a fraction. “Much appreciated.”

And just like that, he was in.

He stepped past the gates, the cool shadow swallowing him whole, and let out a breath he hadn’t realized he’d been holding.

Wasn’t so hard.

He hadn’t even made it ten paces into the city before the stares started.

Phainon kept his stride easy, his chin lifted just so, a casual little half-smile playing on his mouth. The streets of Kremnos stretched wide and clean ahead of him, paved in pale stone that flashed white in the sun. Vendors called out their wares in the distance—bronze, spice, cured meat, armament —their voices carrying clearly through the heat. But it wasn’t the goods they were hawking that caught attention now.

It was him.

Eyes tracked him from under helmets and behind market stalls. Quick glances, sharp and assessing. Some bold, some subtle. All the same look: foreigner.

Didn’t matter that he was dressed for the part. Cipher had made sure of that. She’d cobbled together a passable Kremnoan outfit in record time, pulling in favors from traveling tailors and gods-knew-who-else. A toga-styled garment, loosely draped over one shoulder and cinched at the waist. The inner fabric a deep, rich purple—too rich—and a few sharp, deliberate cuts along the hem and sides gave it a touch of easy, languid nobility. Exactly what Aglaea had warned him not to wear.

The gold laurel wreath adorning his hair probably wasn’t helping.

Neither was the delicate gold anklet around his left leg, shaped like a twisting vine in bloom. Cipher had laughed when she’d pressed it into his palm. “For luck,” she’d said, but he knew her too well. Luck had nothing to do with it. She wanted a favor. And now, thanks to this little ensemble, he probably owed her two.

Aglaea had nearly lost composure over it. Muttering about the Kallion Oath and blood-soaked streets. “One thread out of place in that city and we risk war,” she’d snapped, smoothing her hair with a hand that, for the first time since Phainon had known her, trembled faintly at the wrist.

Still. He’d worn it. He was here.

And it was immediately clear how poorly it landed.

Too fine a drape. A touch too perfumed for Kremnos, a city that valued strength above all. Here, men’s clothes (usually) clung close to the body, practical and built for bloodshed or training grounds. No indulgent silks. No suggestive cuts. No gold wreaths unless you’d taken a city for the gods.

So yes—they recognized him. Or at least, they suspected.

The Deliverer of Okhema might’ve left his formal regalia behind, but the face was the same. The city hadn’t forgotten, even two years after the ink dried on the Kallion Oath—a fragile peace held together by Aglaea’s intervention and the Titan’s own mercy.

Phainon just smiled through it. As if he didn’t feel the weight of every stare.

“Well… that could’ve gone worse.” he muttered under his breath, letting the sarcasm warm his throat.

And he kept walking.

He was here for a casual visit.

That was the line, anyway. Just a simple trip, a friendly neighbor stopping by to see the famed war coliseums and blood gardens.

And if you believed that, you were a damn fool.

Everyone in Kremnos knew better. Hell, he knew better. The only person deluded enough to pretend otherwise was Aglaea, and even she had the decency to grit her teeth when she said it out loud.

The truth hung in the air as thick as the heat rising from the marble streets.

The Flame Chase Journey loomed on the horizon. And like it or not, Phainon needed that prince.

The Crown Prince, Mydeimos. A royal born with gold in his veins, a war god’s own lineage and a blade that never dulled. They’d sent envoys. Invitations. Summons. Cipher even floated a few carefully worded bribes through less official channels. Every message was met with the same reply:

No.

And it didn’t help that only a handful of years before, Kremnos and Okhema had been at war—a brutal, bloody conflict older than Mydeimos himself, fought by men Phainon barely remembered and kings now long dead. No peace treaty, no matter how delicately brokered, erased that.

Coming here officially would’ve been a disaster. If Okhema’s Deliverer strolled in carrying a formal request to drag their heir halfway across the world for a suicidal pilgrimage, it’d be a matter of days before Queen Gorgo and King Eurypon had his head displayed on a pike on top of Nikador’s statue. They hadn’t been particularly impressed with him during his last brief encounter at Aglaea’s side either—Phainon still vividly remembered Gorgo’s cool, imperious gaze and Eurypon’s dismissive grunt when he spoke.

So Aglaea had come up with a workaround.

A casual visit.

And why him? Out of all the well-bred nobles and born diplomats Okhema could’ve sent?

Simple. Phainon was the most disarming of them all—too ‘simple’ to be a real threat, too charming to outright refuse. And, more importantly, there was history. The kind that stretched far enough back Phainon honestly doubted Mydeimos remembered it. Still. Even if he didn’t…

At least he’d get to see the prince again.

He let that thought settle in his chest as he ducked into a small open-air shop lining the street. Baskets of bronze trinkets and leather amulets hung from poles, swaying in the heat. The vendor barely spared him a glance, busy carving a symbol into a flat piece of stone. Phainon wandered over, offering one of his smiles that usually softened stony expressions.

He picked up a small, spear-shaped charm—cast in dull iron, rough around the edges, but something about it caught his eye.

“How much for this one?” he asked, Kremnoan tongue rolling a little too smoothly off his lips.

The old woman looked up. Her gaze landed on the gold laurel at his temple, the purple flash of his inner garment, and then his face. The moment stretched.

Too long.

Phainon’s smile wavered.

“…A gift, perhaps,” he offered, placing the charm back down and brushing his fingertips over a set of carved runes nearby. “Is this Nikador’s mark? Or —”

The entire shop shifted.

A man at the next stall turned his head. A girl carrying a basket of figs paused mid-step. The old vendor stiffened, her weathered mouth flattening into a line.

It hit him a beat too late.

Ah.

He wasn’t supposed to touch that. Or maybe it was what he’d said. Or how he’d said it.

“…What?” Phainon blinked, still smiling, confused.

A muttered string of clipped, annoyed Kremnoan spat at him like a curse. He caught foreigner, soft-palmed, gold-bleeder. Several heads turned. Someone at his shoulder grunted a threat in his ear he couldn’t quite catch.

And then—a firm hand on his shoulder, shoving him toward the street.

Phainon stumbled out into the sunlight, laughing under his breath as a sharp voice barked after him. He wasn’t fluent enough to translate the whole thing, but he was pretty sure it boiled down to get lost.

Well.

He dusted himself off, glancing up at the marble spires in the distance.

Looked like he had his work cut out for him.

By the time the sun slid low enough to stain the white stone streets in gold, Phainon had managed to secure a place to stay.

It wasn’t much—a modest guesthouse tucked between a weaponsmith and a dye shop, the kind of place respectable Okheman diplomats would sneer at and Cipher would call authentic. The matron who ran it hadn’t been thrilled to rent him a room, her gaze lingering on his laurel a little too long, but money was money. And Kremnos respected a man who paid in gold without haggling.

The room was small. Clean, though. A narrow cot, a basin, and a single shuttered window that overlooked a narrow alley where young soldiers laughed and drank until the moon came up.

Phainon dropped his satchel onto the cot, rolled his shoulders, and let out a breath.

Alright. Attempt one. The Coliseum.

Why the Coliseum? Well—it was one of Kremnos’ grandest, most famed public arenas. A towering ring of marble and iron where men bled for glory and the gods’ favor. Half the city gathered there by sunset for duels, war games, and Nikador-only-knows what else (Get it?).

If he was going to pose as a harmless traveler, might as well hit the top attractions. And it didn’t hurt that he’d overheard a vendor mutter earlier about the young prince attending the evening bouts. Apparently, the Crown Prince frequented the place. Often.

Phainon grinned to himself as he fastened the golden anklet around his calf again, pulling the draped folds of his garment into place.

“See, Aglaea,” he murmured, glancing at his reflection in the tiny mirror propped against the wall. “This counts as blending in.”

Even if half the street had stared daggers into him when he passed, and an old man spat at his feet for the perfumed foreigner stink.

Whatever.

Coliseum it was.

Getting there was a trial all its own.

Kremnos wasn’t a city built for strangers. The streets curved and climbed like the ribs of some ancient beast, narrow alleys that abruptly ended in sheer drops or opened into sprawling squares. Every man on the road seemed to have somewhere urgent to be—and no patience for someone blocking their path. Phainon spent more time dodging shoulder checks and cold stares than actually walking.

By the time he reached the outer edge of the Coliseum, the sun hung low in the sky, throwing long shadows across the gleaming marble. The structure was immense, a massive open ring of stone and iron, white columns stretching into the clouds, the distant ring of weapons clashing carrying out over the walls. Banners in crimson and black snapped high above, emblazoned with Nikador’s sigil.

Phainon let out a low breath. Finally.

He approached a vendor hawking drinks outside the entrance—cups filled with some dark thing. Phainon flashed his easy smile and held up a finger. The man narrowed his eyes, named a price at least double what it should’ve been, and Phainon didn’t even flinch. He tossed the coins over. Not worth fighting.

The drink was vile. Bitter and thick with something that clung to the back of his throat like wet bark. He coughed. A group of men leaning against a pillar nearby snorted and muttered under their breath, not bothering to lower their voices.

Phainon just offered them a lazy two-fingered salute and kept walking.

Inside, the air was dense with the metallic tang of blood. The stands were packed—a writhing sea of spectators draped in dark cloaks, some already shouting bets or jeering down at the arena. Sunlight struck off a thousand bare blades, the ring of steel and the roar of the crowd mixing into something that made Phainon’s skin prickle.

He let his gaze lift to the Royal Box—elevated above the masses, shadowed beneath thick red banners. Perfect view of the sand-stained floor below. But it was empty.

Phainon’s brow furrowed. Was he wrong?

After all that?

But the roar of the crowd surged suddenly, a wave of noise, and he caught the glint of bronze helms and bare chests clashing below. The match had already started.

He cursed under his breath.

Well, you’re here now.

Rolling his metaphorical sleeves up, Phainon squared his shoulders and prepared to wade into the wall of people for a front-row view. If I bleed out before I see the prince, my ghost better haunt this damn place.

It took hell and a half to get to that seat.

Phainon had braved elbows, shoulders, insults muttered just loud enough for him to hear, and what might’ve been a half-hearted attempt to trip him on the stairs. At one point, a wiry old man nearly jabbed him in the gut with a walking stick when he tried to squeeze past. He offered his brightest, most apologetic grin and sidestepped the jab. Kremnos didn’t make anything easy.

But damn it, he got the seat.

Wedged between two burly spectators who barely acknowledged his existence, Phainon settled in, the coarse stone warm beneath him from hours of sun. From here, he had a decent view of the arena, close enough to make out the dust kicked up by every step, the rippling muscles, the sharp glint of knuckles connecting with bone.

He expected anything. Two brawny men, some hulking champion, a pack of wild animals. But no.

No, of course not.

Why?

The Crown Prince himself was in the pit.

Phainon blinked. His jaw nearly dropped.

There he was—Mydeimos of Kremnos, bare-chested save for a simple wrap across his knuckles, sweat slicking his hair to his brow, golden eyes cold as struck coin as he drove his fist into another man’s jaw. The crack was audible even from here. The other fighter stumbled back, blood flying, but Mydei didn’t hesitate. He moved like a panther—no hesitation.

Phainon exhaled a low, almost incredulous laugh. Well, my lucky day.

He’d come to chase a ghost of a maybe-past, and instead landed himself a front-row seat to watch the very prince he needed beating the living hell out of someone.

And gods, he’d grown up.

Taller now. Shoulders broad with that hard-cut soldier’s build Kremnos prized. Face sharper—handsome in a way that felt almost unfair, like something carved, all sculpted angles and those impossibly beautiful eyes. Phainon felt something in his chest twinge, his smile softening despite himself.

Good for him.

He should’ve left it at that. Watched, taken mental notes, maybe waited for the fight to end and figured out how to talk to him later.

But then—then those gold eyes turned.

Phainon swore, for a second, that Mydeimos sensed something. In the middle of a brutal match, with sweat on his brow and a crowd roaring in his ears, the prince’s gaze snapped up. Directly to him.

Their eyes met.

Gold to blue.

Phainon felt it like a gut punch.

Time stuttered for a moment. The roaring of the crowd dulled. Phainon’s grin faltered, a flicker of heat climbing the back of his neck. Because Mydei didn’t just look. He stared. That sharp, unflinching stare that pinned a man in place and made him feel like his skin didn’t quite fit right.

Phainon swallowed.

And then—to make matters worse—Mydeimos’ gaze dropped.

Not to the sands. Not to the bloodied man still swaying on his feet before him.

To him.

To the draped folds of Phainon’s toga-styled garment, the rich purple catching in the light like something obscene in a city built on discipline and earth-tones. The laurel wreath caught a glint of sun. The faint curve of the gold anklet flashed when he shifted his weight.

Phainon caught the prince’s brow twitch.

Small. Barely there. A flicker of something unreadable that pulled at the edge of his mouth.

A rare, sharp spark of embarrassment prickled at the back of Phainon’s neck.

Yeah… alright. It’s too gaudy. Should’ve gone with the duller one. The gray. Or that ugly tan Cipher tried to push on me.

He tugged at the edge of the fabric self-consciously. But then—and gods above, why always then—Phainon did the dumbest possible thing.

He raised a hand.

Just a little.

A casual, idiotically cheerful little flick of his fingers. The kind you gave to a neighbor you barely knew, or a child passing in the street. And then— because apparently one bad decision wasn’t enough—he tacked on a thumbs up.

Why.

Why in the gods’ names—

Mydeimos didn’t react right away. His face didn’t so much as flinch.

But Phainon saw it.

That momentary stone-cold hardening of those gold eyes. The twitch of a brow, almost imperceptible. And then—pointedly, without a word—the prince turned his head away.

And immediately drove his fist harder into his opponent. A brutal, teeth-rattling hit.

Phainon blinked.

Well. Alright then.

Maybe not a great idea.

What he didn’t know—what he couldn’t possibly guess, because his own stubborn, blithely casual perspective refused to let him—was that down in that arena, Mydeimos was, in fact, quietly losing his mind.

Because the man he’d spent years—years—secretly, miserably crushing on since childhood had just appeared like some half-drunk sun god, in far-too-rich Kremnoan garb, collarbone and forearms out, hair damp from heat and sticking to his brow.

And then waved at him. And gave him a damn thumbs up.

Like he was still that scrawny, bloodied kid clutching a splintered practice sword and looking up at him like he was anything.

Phainon, of course, caught none of it.

He just leaned back in his seat, let out a low whistle, and took another sip of that awful drink.

“Huh,” he muttered, half to himself, watching as Mydeimos fought even harder now, each blow a little sharper, a little faster, a little more brutal.

The crowd roared.

The men on either side of him muttered something in irritation—something about foreign fools, and watch where you smile, idiot—but Phainon barely noticed.

He just grinned, one elbow slung over the back of his stone seat.

Lucky day, indeed.

The fight eventually ended with a final blow—Mydeimos driving his fist hard into the other man’s gut, sending him sprawling onto the blood-dusted sand. The crowd roared its approval, a guttural, rising sound that shook the air itself.

Phainon winced on the poor bastard’s behalf.

Well. That was that.

Mydeimos didn’t linger over his victory. He raised a hand—a simple, quick gesture of acknowledgment, palm angled toward the stands. It sent the crowd into fresh cheers, a low chant of his name rising and falling like a tide.

But not once did he look at Phainon again.

Not a flicker of a glance. Not a bat of his eyelashes. Nothing

Phainon let out a quiet, breathy laugh through his nose, shaking his head to himself.

Alright. Stonewalling me. Cute.

A little petty, maybe. But… cute.

It shouldn’t have stung. Really, it shouldn’t have. He wasn’t here for Mydei’s attention—not like that, anyway. He had a mission. Bigger things.

But that pointed cold-shoulder landed its blow cleaner than any fist.

Phainon rolled his shoulders, let it slide off. Or tried to.

The prince strode out of the arena, long strides carrying him through the sand archway without breaking pace as his guard fell in around him.

The crowd stayed, murmuring, buzzing with the aftershock of the fight.

Phainon took one last sip of his drink, made a face, and stood.

Time to get to work.

It took a small eternity and no fewer than three accidental elbow jabs to the ribs to make it through the congested stone passageways and down into the lower tiers.

He caught a glimpse—a flash of blonde hair—ahead.

There.

Without thinking, he started weaving his way through the press of people, half-raising his hand in a loose, casual wave. “Hey—”

A broad, armored figure stepped squarely into his path.

Phainon nearly collided with him.

The guard didn’t even look at him.

“Private audience,” the man grunted. “The Crown Prince doesn’t receive visitors without cause.”

Phainon’s jaw twitched.

Gods, it would’ve been so easy. So easy to let something slip from his tongue. A pointed quip, a half-smile paired with some remark about Kremnoan hospitality.

But Aglaea’s voice hissed at the back of his mind: One thread out of place in that city and we risk war.

So.

He swallowed it down. Smoothed his face into something warm, genial, harmless.

“Of course,” he said, all polite grace, and stepped aside.

But not before his gaze caught, just for a second, on the scene beyond the guard.

Mydeimos had slowed his steps. A small cluster of men closed in around him—not soldiers. Friends.

Phainon didn’t need long to guess which one was Hephaestion. Broad-shouldered, bronze-skinned, laugh too easy, the kind of man whose hand clapped Mydeimos on the shoulder and earned, unbelievably, the faintest curl of a smile from the prince.

Phainon’s gut twisted.

He looked away before it could settle.

Whatever. It didn’t matter. This was a long game.

As he turned back toward the city streets, sun already starting to dip, Phainon sighed under his breath.

“Well,” he muttered to himself, “attempt one was a learning experience.”

Another sigh.

“Attempt two’s where I reclaim my dignity”

And with that, he vanished into the crowd.

Attempt Two did not go better.

In fact, it might’ve gone worse.

Phainon, to his credit, tried. At least three times.

First time?

At the market square—easy, right? He figured maybe he could spot the prince doing something utterly mundane, like selecting olives or verbally decimating a fish vendor. What he got instead was a grizzled merchant barking “Okheman’s pay double” before shortchanging him, and no prince in sight. Solid start.

Second time?

The sparring grounds. Word around town was that Mydeimos trained there at least twice a week. Phainon loitered by the fences, made small talk with a trio of soldiers (one of whom kept eyeing his clothes like he was a goat in silk), and waited.

The prince didn’t show.

A kid offered to ‘fetch him for a price.’ Phainon paid.

The kid pocketed the coin and vanished.

Naturally.

Third time?

Desperation made a man creative. Phainon called in a handful of favors, slipped coin where it mattered, and managed to wrangle a formal audience. Official, scheduled, documented. Gods be good.

It lasted ten seconds.

Maybe twelve if you counted the time it took for Mydeimos to walk in.

And Phainon—exhausted, irritable, and fed up with the cold-shoulder act— opened with what in hindsight might not have been the best line.

“You’re really making this difficult, little prince.”

And for a flicker, just a fraction of a heartbeat, something happened.

A twitch.

A barely-there tension around the eyes.

A flare of something dark and utterly indecipherable.

And then?

Without a word, without so much as a goddamn blink, Mydeimos turned, gestured for the guards, and walked right the fuck out.

Phainon was left standing there in a cold, empty chamber, utterly bewildered and a little mortified.

He didn’t know what he’d done wrong.

Not really.

Not then.

And now?

Now this is where it landed him.

Smack dab in the middle of the palace throne room, looking down like a scolded schoolboy. The hall was towering—a vault of pale marble, iron standards hanging from the beams, every banner a crimson red.

And at the far end, seated like war gods judging the unworthy, were Queen Gorgo and King Eurypon.

Neither of them spoke.

Neither of them needed to.

The unimpressed look on their faces was a language unto itself.

Phainon sighed. Ran a hand through his hair.

Shit. He fucked up.

To his credit, he didn’t squirm.

Phainon sat with his back straight, hands resting loosely on his knees, and met their stares with a practiced calm he’d perfected over years of dinners and tense post-battle negotiations. He even managed a polite, if somewhat strained, smile.

Across the hall, Queen Gorgo sat with all the glacial elegance of a carved statue. King Eurypon was just behind her left side—looming.

The unspoken message hung in the room thick as fog: We know why you’re here. And we don’t like it.

Gorgo spoke first.

Her voice was soft. Cold as fresh-forged steel plunged in ice.

“I trust Castrum Kremnos has… met your expectations, Deliverer.”

Phainon inclined his head. “It’s a beautiful city, Your Majesty.”

She hummed. A small, humorless sound. “You seem to be making yourself quite comfortable in it.”

There was a flicker of amusement in her gaze, like she was daring him to play innocent.

Phainon thanked Tribbie in his head for making him study royal etiquette before he left Okhema. He knew better than to argue. Or apologize. Or offer excuses. Kremnoans weren’t fond of excuses.

“I’m grateful for your people’s hospitality,” he replied. “Even if I suspect the price of wine’s doubled since I arrived.”

Eurypon gave a low, dry snort at that. A fraction of approval, maybe. Or not.

Gorgo didn’t smile.

“And yet,” she went on, “I wonder what brings Okhema’s Deliverer so far from his home.”

“I’m not here in any official capacity,” Phainon replied, as evenly as he could. “Just a casual visit.”

He was careful not to glance at Eurypon. Or at the ceremonial axe leaning against the wall behind him.

“I see,” Gorgo murmured. “And in your casual wanderings, you seem to find yourself… frequently in my son’s path.”

“That was never my—”

“Little prince has grown up, hasn’t he?” Phainon blurted, then immediately bit down on the inside of his cheek.

Shit.

Too late.

The queen’s brows arched. Eurypon let out a long-suffering sigh, one hand scrubbing over his jaw.

Phainon fumbled. “I meant—Crown Prince. Crown Prince Mydeimos. He’s, ah—”

“Hopeless,” Eurypon muttered, not to Phainon but to some far-off, exasperated god.

There was a weight to that word.

Something Phainon didn’t quite catch.

Gorgo studied him in silence for a long, heavy beat. Then—and maybe it was a trick of the light, maybe not—something in her expression softened. Just a crack. Not warmth. Resignation, perhaps.

“If it weren’t for my son’s… liking of you,” she murmured, almost to herself, “I’d have cleaved you in half by now.”

Phainon blinked.

“Pardon?”

But before he could puzzle that one out, Eurypon grunted. “You’re dismissed.”

Phainon didn’t argue. He stood, gave a crisp, shallow bow, and turned on his heel.

As he left the hall, he thought—not for the first time—that he might actually end up hanged before this trip was over.

Kephale help him, he still didn’t know what he’d done wrong.

Phainon was about ready to give up.

Today was the day of the Festival of Nikador—the grandest of Kremnos’ yearly rites. A day when warriors, veterans, and would-be heroes gathered in droves to pay blood and praise to the Strife God. When the streets thundered with drumbeats and the clang of sparring blades, and fire-eaters stalked between banners. A city of conquerors celebrating the ancient covenant of war.

You’d think, under those blood-red skies and amidst all that glorious chaos, this would be the perfect place for Phainon to mingle.

It was not.

He barely made it through the first hour before some swaggering local bruiser with more brawn than sense took offense to his everything. Phainon hadn’t even said anything provocative. The man had just declared him scum and challenged him on the spot.

It was supposed to be a quick, harmless scuffle.

It wasn’t.

Phainon ducked one punch, tripped the man by reflex, and the poor bastard landed face-first in a pile of red-dyed festival garlands.

The onlookers howled.

And just like that—he’d humiliated a local in public.

Result: minor notoriety, immediate price hikes, and a running tally of dirty looks. Everything cost thrice as much now. Ale, food, festival trinkets. He even caught one stallkeeper muttering “Deliverer my ass” under his breath.

Phainon sighed, massaging his temple. Perfect.

Well—if there was one good thing to come of this minor disaster…

“Ready to move to the next quarter?” a voice asked beside him.

He glanced over. The stranger was maybe a little older than Mydeimos, gentle

looking, sun-browned, with a crooked nose that had been broken once and a smile that looked far too amused by Phainon’s entire existence.

Ptolemy, that was it.

They’d literally run into each other not long after the garland incident— Phainon half-distracted looking for a drink vendor that wouldn’t triple-charge him, Ptolemy weaving through the crowd carrying some grilled skewers. To his mild shock, instead of swearing at him, the man had recognized who he was. And instead of a challenge or a glare, Ptolemy had asked about Okhema.

Actual curiosity. A minor miracle.

They’d stuck together since.

In the space of an hour, Ptolemy had not only steered him clear of several pickpockets and a would-be knife duel, but also taken it upon himself to help locate one of Phainon’s missing anklets. Somewhere along the way, it had come loose—and if Cipher found out he’d lost it in a festival crowd, Phainon would never hear the end of it.

The man even waved away the merchants charging him extra.

Phainon might’ve actually made his first friend in Kremnos.

It also didn’t hurt that, walking beside Ptolemy, the dirty looks lessened and more than a few warriors gave him respectful nods.

Maybe this night wasn’t a total loss after all.

Phainon spotted it like a man dying of thirst spotting an oasis.

“There,” he muttered, eyes narrowing.

Sure enough—the damned anklet, gleaming faintly gold in the dirt, just beneath the edge of a merchant’s stall piled high with spice baskets.

“Finally,” he breathed, already moving.

“Wait, hold on—” Ptolemy called, but Phainon was already ducking through the crowd.

It should’ve been simple. Quick grab, a sheepish thanks to the vendor, back to drinking overpriced festival wine.

It was not.

The anklet glinted in the lamplight as someone’s boot swung out, accidentally kicking it. It slid a few feet, clinking against a stone.

Phainon hissed a curse. “No, no, no—”

He made to follow, weaving past a pair of laughing women with painted faces. His fingers brushed it—only for a passing child chasing a paper wind-dragon to step right in front of him, the anklet bouncing away again.

“Oh, come on—”

It was absurd, really. A ridiculous, petty chase through a sea of bodies and firelight. At one point, the anklet rolled beneath a table where three warriors were deep in a drinking contest, sloshing their cups as they cheered. At another, a passing dancer’s trailing sash knocked it back into open view.

It became a game of near-misses. Every time Phainon reached for it, someone would block his way—an elderly vendor waving roasted chestnuts, a priest of Nikador singing an old hymn, a pair of lovers not watching where they were going.

And then—because the gods had a sense of humor—a Droma came barreling through.

And of course—of course—its hooves struck the anklet, sending it skittering through the air like a coin flipped by fate.

It landed somewhere deep in the heart of a private, roped-off courtyard lit by hanging lamps. A space guarded by posted soldiers and clearly meant for the city’s upper echelon.

Phainon stared, deflated. “You have got to be kidding me.”

“Well,” Ptolemy said, clapping him on the back. “At least it stopped moving.”

Phainon groaned. “I am going to drown myself in the river.”

“Not yet,” Ptolemy grinned. “Lucky for you, I know the way. Follow me.”

They slipped around the edge of the courtyard, ducking past a cart stacked with amphorae. Ptolemy exchanged a few quiet words with a guard, who rolled his eyes but let them through.

The exclusive space was quieter. The noise of the festival was dulled here, replaced by the soft hum of stringed instruments and the occasional low conversation.

And there was the anklet.

It had landed neatly at the base of a seated figure’s feet. A man, busy tuning a lyre. His expression bored, until he glanced down at the little golden thing by his sandal.

Phainon was already raising a hand. “Apologies, I didn’t mean—”

Before he could finish, Ptolemy’s face lit up. “Peucesta!” he called.

The man looked up, and for the first time Phainon got a good look at him. Lean and sharp in the face, disinterested.

Peucesta arched a brow. Then—with the barest flicker of a smile—he twisted his foot, lightly kicking the anklet away.

It slid.

Phainon’s jaw clenched. “You’ve got to be—”

He followed its arc with his eyes, about to say something sharp—and stopped dead.

Because it had landed by another pair of shoes.

Familiar ones.

Metallic, dusty from the arena sand. And above them—the tall, unmistakable figure of Mydeimos, standing in conversation with another man Ptolemy casually referred to as Leonnius.

Phainon’s throat went dry.

He hadn’t even realized the prince was here.

Mydeimos looked good. Unfairly so. The light caught in the stray strands of his hair, jaw set in a thoughtful line as he listened to Leonnius speak. His posture still and sharp, one hand resting against his hip, the other holding a cup of something red.

Phainon felt his stomach twist in a way he didn’t particularly like.

Peucesta let out a soft, flat “Oops.”

Phainon didn’t move.

Because Mydeimos was about to turn.

His gaze landed on Phainon.

A pause.

Then—the prince’s first actual word to him.

“…Deliverer?”

Phainon’s stomach dropped clean through the floor.

And because gods were cruel and he was stupid, his body moved before his brain caught up.

“Hey!” Phainon heard himself say, too bright, striding forward like they were old friends running into each other at a vineyard. “Nice to see you again—what a coincidence.”

And then—and may he be struck down by Nikador himself—Phainon reached out and clapped the prince on the shoulder.

It was awkward. It was so, so awkward.

Mydeimos stiffened.

Phainon, feeling his own soul leave his body, immediately bent down— snagging the damned anklet at the prince’s feet in one swift motion.

“Anyway,” he muttered, ducking his head, face burning as he backed up. “Got what I came for.”

He made it two steps before Peucesta let out a long, low whistle.

Ptolemy visibly winced, rubbing a hand down his face.

Leonnius coughed into his cup, a sound entirely too amused to be polite. “You must be Phainon,” he said at last.

Phainon grimaced, schooling his expression into something passable as charm. “The one and only.”

Peucesta gave him a slow, lingering once-over, then snorted. “So you’re the Deliverer, huh? Taller than you, isn’t he?”

Phainon blinked, glancing between them. “Is… that relevant or…?”

He trailed off as Mydeimos’s eye twitched again. The others exchanged glances. An inside joke. One Phainon wasn’t in on.

And this would’ve been it, wouldn’t it? His perfect window. The ideal opening to strike up a conversation, finally make his case, deliver his proposal, anything.

But no. No, his dignity was in tatters, and his soul was halfway down the river.

“I should probably—” Phainon began, edging back toward Ptolemy.

“Nonsense,” Ptolemy grinned, entirely too cheerfully, clapping a firm hand between his shoulder blades and guiding him down into a seat nearby. “Let us help.”

Phainon flailed mentally, awkwardly lowering himself onto the bench, still clutching the anklet like a lifeline. The table was suddenly very full of people he did not know and did not trust, except maybe Ptolemy.

And then nothing happened for a second.

The music played. A cup was refilled. Mydeimos hadn’t moved.

Until Leonnius, not even glancing up from his drink, nudged out a booted foot and smacked it against the back of the prince’s leg.

Mydeimos shot him a glare.

Leonnius raised a brow, the look he returned speaking volumes.

Get your shit together, boy.

Mydeimos sighed.

And then—to Phainon’s utter horror—the prince crouched in front of him.

Phainon forgot how to breathe.

Because Mydeimos, silent and unreadable, reached out—took the anklet from his hand—and began fixing the clasp with careful fingers.

Phainon made a strangled sound in the back of his throat. His soul left his body. His soul left.

Not a single god in the heavens could help him now.

He finished fastening the anklet with a deft flick of his thumb, the clasp clicking into place. It was a small thing, but his touch had been careful— surprisingly so for a man who swung swords heavier than most livestock and had a stare sharp enough to flay bone.

Phainon cleared his throat, trying for light, a touch of old teasing.

“…Appreciate it, little prince.”

No sooner were the words out than a shift ran through the air—one Phainon, oblivious, didn’t catch.

The silence hit like a dropped blade.

Ptolemy, to his credit, didn’t even pretend not to hear it.

“Damn,” he muttered under his breath.

Mydeimos stilled.

Whatever flicker of warmth that settled in his eyes vanished so fast it might’ve never existed. The line of his shoulders tightened, and when he stood, it was rigid.

“I remembered I had business elsewhere,” Mydeimos said—clipped and perfectly civil. And not looking at him.

He turned before Phainon could speak, before he could explain or laugh it off, or apologize, or gods, anything.

“Mydei, wait—”

But the prince was already walking, the crowd parting instinctively around him.

Phainon sat there for a heartbeat, stunned, blinking after him. The warm ache of embarrassment spread slow in his chest.

He didn’t even realize someone else was approaching until the tall figure of Hephaestion stepped into view—having arrived just in time to see Mydeimos pass him with a short nod and a look of barely restrained frustration.

Hephaestion’s brow furrowed, confusion flickering across his face. Then his gaze shifted to Phainon.

And in that moment, something passed between them.

A knowing clarity that hurt a little more than it should’ve.

It was too quick—the way understanding settled in Hephaestion’s face. He didn’t need to ask. He just knew, because it was Mydei.

Phainon shouldn’t have cared. But a sour, inexplicable flicker twisted in his chest.

Hephaestion crossed his arms loosely. “He’ll be in the gardens,” he said, voice quieter than before.

Phainon didn’t bother asking how he knew. He just swallowed hard and gave a curt nod, a silent thank you as he pushed himself to his feet.

And then, without another word, he moved after the prince.

Mydeimos remembered.

Gods, he remembered.

Years before he was Crown Prince. Before Kremnos’ coliseums sang his name in blood and before Nikador’s priests called him blessed. Before titles and duty. He was no more than a battered, half-dead boy with a broken sword in his hand and a dozen lifeless men at his feet.

A border skirmish, they called it. A footnote in a season’s campaign log. To him, it was the first time he truly understood how fast men could die. How slow the hours felt after, the heat thick with the scent of blood and old copper.

He’d refused to leave them. The other survivors were already marching back to camp, but he stayed. Sprawled in a shallow ravine, thigh bleeding sluggishly, dirt in his mouth, heart clawing against his ribs. The weight of it was crushing—the failure, the loneliness.

And then the boy.

Older than him by some years—rough around the edges, sun-darkened skin, hands like he worked the earth. No insignia, no armor, just a simple sash and a dagger worn smooth by use.

He should have killed him.

Should have drawn the broken blade at his side, or called out a warning. But he didn’t.

Because the boy crouched beside him, and spoke like they were already kin.

“That’s a nasty scrape, little prince.”

He hadn’t said it like an insult. Not even mockery. Just easy, offhand familiarity, like it was a name Mydeimos had always carried. It rankled. It warmed. Both, somehow.

The boy—Phainon, though he wouldn’t learn the name until later—cleaned the wound, tore strips from his own tunic, packed it with something bitter-smelling from a pouch at his belt.

When Mydeimos had tried to get up, to limp back to his men, the older boy had pressed a hand to his shoulder, steady but gentle.

“A dead prince can’t avenge his men. Live long enough to scare them later.”

And Mydeimos remembered the way it made his chest ache. How desperately he wanted to be that—feared, unbroken, worthy of his dead.

He’d stayed there with him. Not for a night. Not for a few stolen hours.

A week.

A week in a forgotten pocket of nowhere, sheltering in a hollowed cave mouth and the sparse cover of gnarled trees. Phainon caught rabbits. Built a fire. Told stupid, half-remembered village ghost stories, shared bruised, stolen fruit from a grove he swore the gods themselves had abandoned.

And Mydeimos had let him.

Listened.

Healed.

He remembered, with sickening clarity, how the ache in his leg dulled, but the ache in his chest only deepened. How every day he felt less like a prince, and more like a boy with no name.

And in the pale hours before dawn on the seventh day, Mydeimos left.

No farewell.

Just the heavy ache of something lodged behind his ribs.

He thought he’d never see him again.

And yet now—a lifetime later—here he was. The same maddening ease. The same damned smile.

Calling him little prince.

And Mydeimos, for all his iron will, all his discipline, still felt like that bloodied boy, pinned between shame and longing.

He loathed it.

He lived for it.

The evening had settled like a cloak, the sky caught in a wash of iron-blue and fading crimson. The statues of Nikador loomed tall between the flowers and olives, sword tips spearing through tangled branches. The scent of crushed earth and oil lamps clung to the air.

Mydeimos sat at the far end of a colonnade, one knee drawn up, his cloak discarded beside him. The waning light painted his profile in sharp planes —gaze fixed on nothing in particular.

Phainon hesitated.

He should leave him be. He knew that. Every instinct, every scrap of experience told him to turn around and quit while he was ahead. But he didn’t.

He crossed the stone path and came to a slow stop beside him, easing down.

A long silence stretched between them.

Phainon let out a small breath, offering a faint smile.

“Didn’t think you were the sentimental type, kid.”

At first, there was no reply.

Then—without turning—

“Stop calling me that.”

Phainon chuckled under his breath. “What, sentimental or kid? I’d say both fit.”

The change was subtle, but immediate.

Mydeimos shifted, straightening just enough to turn his head, gaze catching his.

And then he leaned in.

His voice, when it came, was quiet. Each word like a knife.

“I command armies. I bury men twice my age and twice my strength. I have bled, killed, and carved the names of my enemies into stone while you drank wine in Okhema’s shade.”

Phainon’s smile faltered.

“And you,” Mydeimos went on, his gaze sharp enough to flay skin, “still speak as if I’ve not earned the right to stand at your shoulder.

The words struck clean.

Phainon blinked, thrown for the first time in days. The warmth he wore like a second skin faltered, the ache of something colder settling in its place. He hadn’t expected— hadn’t seen—

“I…” Phainon swallowed, voice quieter now. “I didn’t know.”

No humor left in him.

“I didn’t mean it like that.”

Mydeimos said nothing, but the sharpness in his eyes dulled a fraction. Not softening. But easing the killing edge.

Phainon let out a breath, running a hand through his hair as he shook his head. “Alright,” he murmured. “No more ‘kid.’ You have my word.”

Mydeimos held his gaze a moment longer, then looked away.

Phainon exhaled, scrubbing a hand over his face.

“Right,” he muttered, mostly to himself.

Neither of them spoke.

The war god’s statue cast long shadows across the stone. A drumbeat from the city carried faintly on the wind.

Phainon stayed seated, though part of him itched to leave.

But he didn’t.

Mydeimos stood.

The movement was quiet, but it felt like the whole garden shifted with it.

Phainon glanced up, bracing for another cold dismissal, another silent wall.

Instead, Mydeimos spoke, leaving no room for argument.

“Fine. You’ve got yourself an audience. Tomorrow.”

He turned, pausing just long enough to glance back over his shoulder.

“Don’t disappoint me.”

And then he was gone. A shadow slipping between statues, swallowed by the fading light.

Phainon let out a slow, frayed breath.

Gods.

He sat there another moment, staring after the place where the prince had vanished.

Part of him knew he should scrap the plan. Cut his losses. Report back to Aglaea with nothing but bruised pride and an empty ledger.

But he wouldn’t.

One more shot.

One last chance, come dawn.

Then—whatever came after.

He sighed, hauling himself to his feet.

“Still alive,” he muttered to no one, and followed the garden path back toward the city lights.

Maybe he came a bit early.

Reasonable, really. Any sane man in his position would’ve done the same. It wasn’t paranoia, per se—more like precaution. Because it wasn’t entirely inconceivable that Crown Prince Mydeimos, in all his cold-blooded, ironclad unpredictability, might forgo the whole meeting on a whim. And then where would Phainon be? Back at Okhema with nothing but a spectacular personal failure and a lecture from Aglaea.

So yes—he came early.

Only a little.

The guards at the threshold had clearly not been briefed, judging by the way they’d straightened, exchanged brief glances, and began offering some practiced line about how the prince was not yet prepared to receive—

Phainon had cut them off with a sharp look. A few low, carefully chosen words. A comment about their prince’s impeccable discipline, about how surely he wouldn’t mind a guest of the Deliverer’s… persistent reputation.

And a smile.

That had done it.

A shared, knowing look passed between the guards—equal parts pity and admiration, which was never a good sign—and then one of them had wordlessly led him inside.

Phainon followed, expecting stone walls and a council chamber. A war room maybe, lined with maps and iron-cast weapons. Or one of those blood-drenched shrines they called meeting halls.

What he got was… this.

Prince Mydeimos’s personal quarters.

Dimly lit, heavy with incense, the kind of warm, quiet stillness that felt too intimate for what was supposed to be a political arrangement. And there—a figure reclined half-lazily on an overlarge, fur-draped bed. Long hair unbound and spilling over his shoulder, bare skin catching the amber light. In one hand, a shallow cup, crimson liquid swirling slow and viscous.

Pomegranate. It had to be. Mydei hated wine.

Phainon swallowed.

He hadn’t even known the prince was capable of looking like this. Lounging, half-naked, sharp-edged in the throat and wrist but somehow still softer in this setting but not quite. Like a sated lion still watching it’s prey.

And then—Mydeimos spoke.

Voice low, heavy with sleep yet no less smooth.

“You seemed so eager to meet me.” A lazy sip from the cup. Eyes half-lidded, unreadable. “Why so quiet now, Deliverer?”

Phainon did the only sensible thing a man in his situation could do.

He smiled tightly and lied.

“Didn’t want to wake you.”

“Mhm.”

That was all the prince gave in reply. A soft, disinterested hum, neither agreement nor dismissal—but it was enough.

He straightened, cleared his throat. It was warm in here. Or maybe that was just his own pulse pounding a little too hard in his neck.

“Right—so, I… I won’t waste your time,” he started, already painfully aware that he probably was. “I came because—because this isn’t just a visit.”

Mydeimos sipped his drink, gaze fixed on him over the rim. Unblinking.

Phainon pressed on.

“I came because the Flame Chase Journey’s begun. You’d know that by now—all twelve Chrysos heirs tasked with—” he caught himself. Right, no need to explain what they both already knew. “And your name’s on that list.”

Nothing. Not even a flicker of surprise. Of course not.

“And I know there’s… controversy,” he pushed, words starting to tumble faster now. “Over what it means. Killing your own gods, claiming their Coreflames—I know Kremnos has ties to Nikador like no other nation. I understand why you’d hesitate. Why anyone would.”

He was rambling. He could hear it.

“But this isn’t just about that,” Phainon tried, forcing his voice steady. “It’s about what happens next. About what’s left after the Titans fall. Kremnos and Okhema are—we’re on fragile ground. The treaty is young, and no one trusts it’ll hold. You know that as well as I do.”

He took a step closer, hating how desperate it might look, but unwilling to stop.

“I believe if you join the Chase, if you stand beside us—it wouldn’t just strengthen your claim as a hero of your people. It would forge something lasting. Between our nations. Between you and the others. Between you and me.”

Gods, that sounded worse aloud.

Phainon faltered then, words catching in his throat as he stared at the prince’s face—a face that hadn’t changed once during his entire plea. Not a raised brow. Not a twitch of his mouth. Just that infuriatingly serene, detached expression.

He sipped his drink again. Waited.

Phainon felt his voice die out somewhere between his ribs.

Silence settled. Heavy. Long enough for the distant sound of the bloodfall to creep back into the edges of his awareness. Long enough for his own heartbeat to start sounding too loud.

And then, Mydeimos set his cup down. The soft clink was deafening in the quiet.

“This,” the prince said, “is what you woke me up for?”

Not even anger in it. Just cold, flat disappointment.

Phainon swallowed.

Mydeimos stood.

Slowly. No sound but the shift of bare feet and the faint rustle of sheets.

Phainon tensed before he could help it, a lifetime of instinct making his shoulders square as if for a blow. The prince’s drink sat abandoned on the low table now, forgotten.

“You’re not used to being refused, are you?”

The words were soft, but they landed like a thrown dagger.

Phainon let out a breath through his nose, something wry curling at the corner of his mouth. Who was?

“Can’t say I enjoy it,” he admitted.

Mydeimos didn’t answer. Just began circling him in, slow, measured steps.

The room felt too small all of a sudden.

Phainon stayed where he was, watching him sidelong. The tension in the air wasn’t quite hostile. But it wasn’t far from it either. This felt less like a conversation now and more like a fight waiting for a spark.

“If you want something from me, Deliverer,” Mydeimos murmured from behind him, voice pitched low, “you’ll have to earn it.”

Phainon turned, just enough to track him. “And how exactly would you have me do that?”

Mydeimos came to a stop a pace away, head tilting slightly. “Prove you can keep up.”

Phainon’s brow furrowed. That sounded a hell of a lot like—

His gaze flicked to the room. To the rumpled bed. The scattered weapons in the corner. The lack of armor on the prince’s frame.

“Here?” he asked, incredulous. “In your quarters?”

He gestured loosely. “You’re half asleep and half dressed, it’d be dishonorable to—”

“I don’t recall asking your permission,” Mydeimos cut in smoothly.

Phainon opened his mouth to argue, but the other man stepped closer, eyes gleaming faintly in the half-light. “Or,” Mydeimos drawled, “are you afraid?”

Damn it.

Phainon gave a quiet snort, shaking his head. “Fine, fine.” He reached up, shrugging off his outer coat with a fluid motion. The garment caught for a second on the chain around his throat—one of those simple, slender Kremnoan talismans he forgot he even wore—before sliding free.

He didn’t miss the way Mydeimos’s eyes caught on the motion. Or how, for a fraction of a second, his gaze lingered at Phainon’s bared neck before flicking away, face schooled back to perfect neutrality.

Strange.

Phainon flexed his knuckles, grinning despite himself. “Alright then, prince. But don’t cry when you lose.”

Mydeimos blinked.

Then, his mouth curved. Not a smirk, not a grin, but something sharper. A wolfish thing, all teeth and promise.

“Very well.”

That should’ve been his first warning.

They moved at the same time.

Phainon surged forward, aiming to end it quick—a sharp pivot and grab meant to get a hold around Mydeimos’s arm, twist him off-balance and prove a point without leaving a bruise.

But Mydeimos slipped past him like smoke, parrying the reach with a flick of his wrist and a sidestep that left Phainon catching air.

Not bad.

The prince didn’t follow up or press the advantage, just turned smoothly, watching him with that unreadable, half-lidded stare. Unbothered. Almost lazy.

But not careless.

Alright then.

Phainon went again. Faster this time. A feint, then a strike toward the shoulder. It was blocked easily, the sharp crack of wrist meeting wrist sounding in the stillness of the chamber. The force of it ran up Phainon’s arm.

He grinned.

And then they were moving, circling, testing the bounds of each other’s footing. Neither going for a killing blow, but neither playing soft either. Mydeimos fought without wasted motion while Phainon fought with a relaxed, confident looseness.

At one point, Phainon ducked a sharp hook of Mydei’s arm, rolling sideways and yanking down a thick curtain draped over the bedframe. The heavy fabric collapsed in a rush of sound between them, a wall of rich crimson that disrupted the prince’s sightline for half a beat.

Phainon lunged through it—but Mydeimos was already moving.

The low table between them was kicked aside, narrowly missing Phainon’s shin. The thing clattered to the floor and splintered against the far wall.

Titans.

“Hope that wasn’t priceless,” Phainon muttered under his breath.

They closed again, exchanging a quick flurry of blows—a jab, a block, a hook that caught Phainon’s ribs hard enough to sting. He answered with a knee that nearly caught the prince’s hip, only for Mydeimos to pivot away.

Evenly matched. Damn it.

Phainon stumbled back a step, bumping against one of the old wall hangings. He grabbed it for balance—and promptly ripped the thing down as Mydeimos advanced. The fabric coiled around his arm as he let it drop.

“Your interior decorator’s going to hate me.”

Mydeimos didn’t so much as blink.

And then Phainon made his mistake.

He got cocky. That overconfident tilt to his shoulders as he feigned left and went low, sweeping his leg out in a move that worked on a hundred other men.

But Mydeimos wasn’t other men.

The prince caught the motion clean, stepped in with a sharp pivot, and used Phainon’s own momentum against him—seizing him by the arm and shoulder, slamming him hard against the cold stone wall.

A forearm pinned across his chest.

Phainon let out a grunt, blinking up into that impassive face a handspan from his own.

And then, despite himself, he chuckled.

“Titans,” he rasped, “you’ve gotten mean.”

Mydeimos didn’t answer. Just shoved him harder against the wall, the pressure sharp against his sternum, enough to remind Phainon who had the advantage.

His pulse thudded in his ears.

“What’s wrong,” he drawled, “afraid I’ll win next time?”

It was meant to be light—a needle to pry loose another one of those rare smiles.

But Mydeimos didn’t smile.

He let out a breath instead—a quiet, tight sound. Not quite a sigh or scoff. Almost…uncharacteristically soft, like he was tired of chasing a conversation only one of them knew they were having.

“You really don’t get it, do you?”

Phainon’s brow knit, confusion flickering there in the space between their locked gazes. “Get what?”

For a moment, nothing. No answer. Just the rasp of their breathing and the lingering heat of the fight. Mydeimos’s stare didn’t waver—but something behind it faltered. The kind of fracture you almost didn’t catch if you weren’t already looking.

And Phainon was looking now.

Something about the set of Mydeimos’s jaw, the slight tension in his mouth. His grip shifted minutely, like he wasn’t sure whether to let go or hold tighter.

It should’ve ended there. A clipped insult, a sharp dismissal, the usual way these things went. But it didn’t.

Instead, Mydeimos exhaled as if forcing down something long past bearing. His hand came up before Phainon could move, fingers curling at his jaw. Not hard or soft. Just… there.

Phainon stiffened, unprepared for the closeness. The warmth of that touch. The bare, unguarded weight of it.

“Mydei—”

“By Nikador’s tenacity,” the prince muttered, voice strained now, cracking at the edges, “you’re so fucking slow.”

And before Phainon could make sense of that—before the words even properly landed—Mydeimos kissed him.

It wasn’t clean or careful. Just the sudden, certain press of Mydeimos’s mouth against his—tense, restless, and so staggeringly real it cracked the world open.

Phainon froze.

His mind went hollow, all sharpness stripped away. No clever remark, no practiced deflection, nothing but a stunned, brittle stillness.

He felt the faint drag of Mydeimos’s breath, the way the other man hesitated just a fraction too long, as if already regretting it, as if bracing for recoil.

Phainon’s fingers twitched at his sides. His heart kicked against his ribs.

“Though if you really want to tour again,” he murmured, fingers tightening just slightly at Phainon’s waist, enough to make him feel it, “I’ll make sure they behave.”

That shouldn’t have made Phainon shudder—but it did.

He laughed, ducking his head to bite lightly at Mydei’s shoulder in retaliation before shifting the topic with a sly, “Well—”

The grin tugging at the corner of his mouth betraying how unserious the question was—but he asked it anyway.

“What about your parents?” he asked, fingertips lazily tracing along Mydei’s jaw, brushing the damp hair away from his temple. “Pretty sure they actually do hate me.”

Mydei gave a sound that might’ve been a laugh if it wasn’t so dry. He shifted, one arm tightening loosely around Phainon’s waist.

“They hate more people than they love,” he said. “If they didn’t glare at you, I’d be worried.”

Phainon barked a laugh at that, hand moving to cup Mydei’s cheek. “Really?” he teased, though a flicker of memory surfaced—of Queen Gorgo’s cold, measuring stare, King Eurypon’s unreadable expression like a man already imagining how best to dismantle him in four different ways. He visibly shivered, though he tried to pass it off as nothing.

“Actually… you know what?” he muttered. “Maybe this is a bad idea.”

He didn’t mean it. But damn if it wasn’t a little intimidating.

Mydei’s eye twitched, and he shifted just enough to level a look at him.

“They’ll treat you with the respect you deserve,” he said solemnly, not even being a question.

Phainon’s pulse caught for half a second. It was stupid, how fast his heart kicked up at that—but it did.

And then the humor in his expression faded, just a touch. He exhaled, the air leaving him, thumb stroking once against Mydei’s cheekbone.

“There’s one thing though,” he said, quieter now.

Phainon traced idle circles along Mydei’s spine, the earlier heat softened into something looser. He could’ve stayed like this—half-draped over the other man, the world held at arm’s length.

But it wasn’t his to hold off forever.

He sighed.

And Mydei must’ve felt it, because his hand stilled where it rested against Phainon’s hip. A brief pause. Then, a quiet exhale, less annoyed than resigned. When he moved, it was slow, straightening slightly, the loose sprawl of limbs tightening as he gathered himself.

His face sobered, the warmth bleeding out of his expression by degrees— not cold, but composed. The Crown Prince of Castrum Kremnos once more.

He met Phainon’s gaze, unreadable as ever.

“Speak, Deliverer.”

Not a lover now. The war-forged heir, who carried his nation’s name like a blade.

Phainon swallowed.

He should’ve prepared for this moment. Rehearsed it. Worn one of his strategic smiles and let it carry him through like it always did. But maybe it was the hour, or the ache in his bones, or what they’d just done—but he didn’t have it in him to be anything but honest.

“I could tell you it’s for the whole of Amphoreus,” Phainon sighed. “For everyone and their safety. That if you join us, you’ll be securing peace for generations.”

A pause. He let his hand drop to the sheets, staring at the folds between them like they held answers.

“But the truth is… it’s for me too.”

He didn’t glance up. Couldn’t. Not yet.

“I don’t know if I’m enough for this,” he admitted. “If I can carry it alone. If I even want to anymore.”

A bitter laugh scraped out of him. “I’m supposed to be the Deliverer. I was born with a prophecy wrapped around my throat and meant to carry the weight of the world on my back. But sometimes, gods, I wake up and all I want is to leave it behind. Burn the prophecy. Disappear. Let someone else bleed for it.”

The words felt heavier spoken aloud than they ever had in his head.

“And I’ve never… I don’t ask for things, Mydei. Not like this.” He finally looked up, meeting the other man’s gaze.

No titles now.

“I’m not asking as the Deliverer. Or the Chrysos Heir.”

He drew a breath.

“I’m asking as me.”

Another beat, the night stretching long and silent between them.

“Come with me.”

An invitation.

And for the first time in a long time, Phainon let himself hope.

Mydeimos didn’t answer right away.

He sat there, eyes on Phainon like he was weighing every word, testing them for fractures.

Then, finally—a slow exhale through his nose.

“I’ll consider it.”

Simple. But it meant something, coming from him.

His gaze softened, just barely. “Sleep, Phainon. We’ll speak in the morning.”

Phainon huffed a tired laugh, everything finally catching up to him at once. He let his head drop back to the pillow, every muscle gone loose and spent.

“Didn’t know you could order a man to sleep,” Phainon mumbled, his voice already exhausted.

Mydei didn’t bother replying. Just stayed where he was, one arm draped heavy across Phainon’s waist, his gaze somewhere distant.

The room settled with the soft drag of breath, and the faint cooling of sweat-damp skin.

Phainon’s lashes fluttered. Sleep pulled at him slow, like tide against shore.

And just as the dark started to take him, something brushed his ear—low, quiet, meant for no one but the night.

“There’s little I wouldn’t do for you.”

A warmth in his chest, a tug at his heart.

Phainon smiled, eyes already shut.

Darkness took him.

The sun poured warm and golden through the open arches of the chamber, bathing the marble floor of Okhema’s hall in light. Scrolls lay unrolled across the polished table, ink still fresh on the latest decree.

Aglaea stood at its head, one hand poised on the carved edge, eyes skimming the official seal of Kremnos pressed in crimson wax beside their own.

“A formal alliance,” she murmured aloud, voice smooth but carrying a sharp, pleased undercurrent. “The Crown Prince of Kremnos joins the Flame Chase Journey, and with him, his nation’s full protection over Okhema until its conclusion. A declaration of unity, binding in fire and blood.”

She let the words settle, a small, knowing smile curving the corner of her mouth.

“Well, Phainon,” Aglaea said without lifting her gaze from the parchment, “I would ask how you managed it, but I think I’d rather hear you admit it.”

Phainon, lounging far too casually in a chair nearby with a bottle of wine, choked.

Spluttering, he set the cup down too fast and avoided her gaze. A flush rose to his face, trailing from his cheeks to the tips of his ears.

“I—” He cleared his throat. “I earned it.”

Aglaea’s brow arched.

At that moment, Cipher passed through the chamber toying with a coin, glancing between them. She grimaced, sighing as if physically pained.

“I’m not getting that outfit back, am I?”

Phainon elbowed her in passing without a word, his face still pink.

Aglaea let the moment linger, savoring it like fine wine before setting the parchment down with deliberate grace.

“Remind me to commission a temple in your honor, should we live to see the end of this madness,” she mused, voice rich with dry amusement.

Phainon groaned, rubbing a hand down his face. “Terrible idea.”

Without missing a step, Cipher’s voice drifted from the corridor. “I’ll start on the statue.”

A ripple of irreverent laughter stirred the air, light as sunlight against stone.
